# INTRODUCTION

This report describes my internship experience at Micromax, where I worked on the development of an Emergency Response System (ERS). Micromax is a technology company located in Unanderra, New South Wales. The ERS project was created to improve workplace safety, especially for employees who may be working alone or in areas where other staff cannot immediately notice an emergency. The purpose of the system is to act as a "second person" by detecting emergency events and sending alerts to the right people as quickly as possible. The system combines manual emergency triggers, sensor-based fall detection, multi-channel notifications, and incident logging.

During my placement, I was involved in the design and development of a functional ERS prototype. My role included working with embedded devices, server-side software, database storage, alert functions, and a real-time dashboard. The system used Raspberry Pi Pico/Pico W devices as client devices and a Raspberry Pi 5 as the central server. The client devices were responsible for detecting emergency inputs, such as a panic button press or fall detection from the MPU6050 sensor. The server then received the emergency data, classified the event, stored the incident information, and triggered suitable alerts such as email, SMS, audio alarms, and relay outputs.

The main goal of my internship was to apply the engineering knowledge I have learned at university to a real workplace project. Through this placement, I aimed to improve my practical skills in embedded systems, IoT communication, Python programming, database design, and system integration. I also wanted to better understand how an engineering prototype is planned, tested, improved, and documented in an industry environment.

The ERS project had several key objectives. It aimed to provide better protection for lone workers, reduce the time needed to respond to emergencies, avoid single points of failure by using multiple alert channels, and clearly separate personal assistance alerts from mass emergency alerts. The project also focused on keeping accurate incident records so that emergency events and notification outcomes could be reviewed later for compliance, reporting, and future improvement.

The rest of this report will discuss the background of the placement, the design and development of the Emergency Response System, the technical tasks I completed, the problems I encountered, and how I solved them. It will also reflect on the skills I developed during the internship and evaluate how this experience contributed to my professional and academic growth.

# COMPANY DESCRIPTION

Micromax is an Australian technology company located in Unanderra, New South Wales. The company was founded in 1960 and has developed from an industrial engineering business into a multi-disciplinary technology group. Today, Micromax provides technology products and solutions across different areas, including healthcare, transport, industrial systems, manufacturing, retail, commercial organisations, mining, and government sectors.

The company operates mainly in the technology and engineering sector. Its work includes embedded computing, IoT systems, industrial communication, power supply solutions, healthcare technology, visitor monitoring, traffic survey tools, and smart monitoring systems. Micromax also has several specialised brands, such as Micromax Technology, Micromax Health, Statronics, sPower, TCS-BI, and TCS Products & Surveys. Each brand focuses on a different part of the business, which allows the company to support a wide range of customers and projects.

Micromax's main strength is that it can provide practical technology solutions from design to deployment. The company combines local engineering experience with support from global technology partners. Its capabilities include custom hardware and electronics, embedded systems, industrial computers, IoT devices, power supplies, UPS systems, converters, battery management, and industrial integration. This means the company is not only selling products, but also helping customers design, integrate, and support complete solutions.

The company's mission and values are closely related to solving real-world problems through technology. From my understanding, Micromax focuses on providing reliable, useful, and industry-ready solutions that can help organisations work more safely and efficiently. The company also has a strong focus on research and development, and it works with education and research institutions such as the University of Wollongong. This connection is important because it supports innovation and gives students opportunities to participate in real engineering projects.

During my placement, I mainly worked on the Emergency Response System project. This project matched Micromax's business direction because it involved embedded devices, IoT communication, server-side processing, smart monitoring, and automated alerts. The purpose of the system was to improve workplace safety, especially for lone workers. The system was designed to detect emergencies, send alerts through different channels, and keep incident records for future reporting and improvement.

Overall, Micromax was a suitable company for my professional placement because its work is strongly connected to my engineering studies. Through this placement, I was able to see how embedded systems, communication technology, software, databases, and user-facing dashboards can be combined into one working system. This helped me understand how engineering knowledge can be used to solve real workplace needs, not only as theory but also as a practical solution.

# WORK DESCRIPTION

During my placement at Micromax, my role was mainly related to the development and testing of the Emergency Response System prototype. I worked as an engineering intern and contributed to both hardware and software parts of the project. My work included understanding the system requirements, testing different communication methods, developing server-side functions, improving the client device logic, and supporting the indoor location estimation feature. The project was designed to provide a "second-person" safety function for staff working alone, so that emergencies could be detected and reported even when no other person was nearby.

At the beginning of the placement, I first learned about the company structure, the main business areas. I reviewed the project requirements and discussed the overall design direction with my mentor and project team. In the first few weeks, I also helped complete the ERS specification document and researched suitable implementation options for the system. This stage helped me understand the expected functions of the system, including personal emergency alerts, mass emergency alerts, fall detection, multi-channel notifications, and incident logging.

One of my main responsibilities was to work on the client device based on the Raspberry Pi Pico/Pico W. I tested the button-triggering logic for different emergency types. For personal emergency, the device used a sustained button press to confirm that the user needed help. For mass emergency, the device used five rapid button presses within a short time window to reduce accidental triggering. I also worked with the MPU6050 sensor for fall detection. The fall detection logic used accelerometer and gyroscope readings to identify a possible fall, and the system included a short cancel window so the user could stop a false alarm if needed.

Another important part of my work was server-side development on the Raspberry Pi 5. I configured and tested the email alert function, SMS alert function, audio alert function, and relay output. When the server received an emergency message from the client device, it needed to classify the event type, store the incident record, and trigger the correct alert workflow. For example, personal emergencies and mass emergencies needed different messages and different response actions. The server also used SQLite to store incident information and logs, which helped make the system more traceable and easier to review later.

I also worked on the communication design between the client device and the server. During the placement, I tested both Wi-Fi and LoRaWAN communication. I configured and tested the Raspberry Pi LoRaWAN gateway and the Pico LoRaWAN transmitter to check whether signals could be sent and received correctly. I researched the advantages and limitations of LoRaWAN and Wi-Fi for this project. LoRaWAN was useful for low-power and long-range communication, while Wi-Fi was useful for faster and more direct IP-based communication. Based on my testing, I improved the client-side communication logic so that the device could try LoRaWAN first and switch to Wi-Fi if transmission failed.

For the LoRaWAN part, I helped design a compact payload format. Instead of sending a long text message from the Pico device, the system used a small event code to represent the emergency type. The Raspberry Pi 5 server then translated the code into a readable event description. This design made the transmitted data smaller and more suitable for LoRaWAN communication. I also helped integrate the LoRa receiving process into the main server workflow, so that LoRa data could be parsed and processed together with other emergency events.

In the later stage of the placement, I worked on the indoor location estimation feature. I researched BLE indoor localisation, RSSI-based distance estimation, trilateration, and fuzzy logic methods. I tested how RSSI values could be used to estimate the device position through multiple gateways. I also helped develop the map-based configuration feature, where users could upload a floor plan, define real-world dimensions, place gateway points, and configure room zones through the web interface. This made the location result easier to understand because the system could show not only coordinates, but also a room name such as office, kitchen, or boardroom.

# EVALUATION

## Experience Learned

During this placement, I learned many technical and professional skills that are difficult to gain only from classroom study. From the technical side, I improved my understanding of embedded systems, IoT communication, server-side programming, database logging, and system integration. The Emergency Response System was not a single software program or a simple hardware circuit. It included client devices, sensors, wireless communication, a Raspberry Pi server, alert functions, a database, and a dashboard. Because of this, I learned how different parts of an engineering system need to work together to produce a reliable result.

I also learned new tools and working methods used in a real workplace. For example, I used GitHub to manage code updates and keep a backup of the project. I also learned to use Jira-style task planning to break a large project into smaller tasks and track progress. These tools helped me work in a more organised way. I gradually built the habit of uploading tested code to GitHub after completing an update, instead of only keeping files locally. This helped reduce the risk of losing work and made later review easier.

This placement also improved my time management and communication skills. Before starting a new stage of work, I learned to plan the main tasks first and create a clear timeline. This helped me avoid working without direction. At the end of each day, I also wrote a short daily summary to record what I completed, what problems I found, and what I planned to do next. This habit made communication with my mentor and team clearer and more efficient. It also helped me reflect on my own progress.

One of the biggest challenges I faced was the BLE indoor location function. In theory, RSSI-based positioning is a workable method because the system can estimate the device location by comparing signal strength values received from different gateways. However, in a real indoor environment, the result was much more difficult to control. Walls, furniture, human movement, and other sources of interference could affect the RSSI values. Also, converting RSSI into distance is not a simple linear process, so a small change in signal strength could cause a large change in the estimated distance. Because of this, it was very difficult to achieve accurate coordinate-level positioning in practice. After practical testing, I learned that it was more realistic to use fuzzy logic and room-based location estimation instead of trying to locate the device at an exact point. Therefore, the system focused on identifying the room or area where the emergency happened, such as the toilet, kitchen, office, or boardroom. This made the location result more reliable and more useful for emergency response.

## Achievements and Milestones

During my placement, one of the main milestones was that the basic emergency response workflow was successfully built and tested. The client device was able to detect different emergency inputs, including personal emergency, mass emergency, and fall detection. The server was then able to receive the emergency data, classify the event type, store the incident record, and trigger suitable alert actions. This was an important achievement because it showed that the main system process could work from the device side to the server side.

Another achievement was the improvement of the system's alert functions. I contributed to testing and configuring different alert methods, including email, SMS, audio alerts, and relay output. These functions helped the ERS provide multi-channel notifications instead of relying on only one alert method. This made the prototype more practical for real emergency situations, where alerts need to be noticed quickly and reliably.

I also achieved progress in the communication part of the system. I tested both LoRaWAN and Wi-Fi communication and helped improve the data transmission design. By using compact event codes, the system could send smaller emergency messages that were more suitable for low-power wireless communication. This helped make the communication process more efficient and easier to manage.

A further milestone was the progress made in indoor location estimation. Through research and practical testing, I found that exact coordinate-level positioning was difficult in a real indoor environment because RSSI values were easily affected by walls, furniture, and other interference. Therefore, the project moved toward a more realistic room-based location approach using methods such as fuzzy logic. This made the location result more useful for emergency response, as staff mainly need to know which area or room the emergency occurred in.

In addition, I made progress in project organisation and documentation. I helped clean and organise project files, improve the folder structure, separate code files from non-code resources, and prepare testing notes for future development. Although these tasks were not direct system functions, they were important for making the project easier to maintain, test, and continue after my placement.

Overall, these achievements show that I was able to contribute to several important parts of the ERS prototype, including emergency detection, alert triggering, communication, location estimation, and documentation. More importantly, I learned how to turn separate technical parts into a more complete and usable engineering system.

## Link to Degree

This placement was strongly connected to my degree in Telecommunications Engineering and Internet of Things. Instead of only learning theories in lectures, I had the opportunity to apply several important areas of my degree to a real engineering project. The Emergency Response System required knowledge from embedded systems, communication networks, IoT design, programming, databases, and engineering project management. This helped me understand how the subjects I studied at university can be used together to build a practical system.

The knowledge from embedded systems was directly applied when I worked on the Raspberry Pi Pico/Pico W client device. In the ERS project, the client device needed to read button inputs, collect data from the MPU6050 sensor, identify emergency events, and send messages to the server. My study in this area helped me understand how a small device can respond to real-time inputs and run event-based logic. This was useful when testing personal emergency triggers, mass emergency triggers, and fall detection.

The knowledge from data communications and wireless communication subjects was also very important. The ERS project used Wi-Fi, LoRaWAN, and BLE, so I needed to consider signal transmission, reliability, latency, interference, and communication range. For example, when comparing LoRaWAN and Wi-Fi, I had to think about which method was more suitable for small emergency messages, low-power devices, and workplace coverage. This helped me connect communication theory with real system design.

The project was also closely related to my IoT learning. The ERS was a typical IoT system because it connected physical devices, sensors, wireless communication, a backend server, a database, and a dashboard. Through this project, I learned that IoT is not only about connecting devices to a network. It also involves collecting useful data, processing events, storing records, sending alerts, and presenting information clearly to users. This gave me a more complete understanding of how an IoT system works from the device level to the application level.

The placement also related to engineering design and project management. During the project, I learned to plan tasks, record daily progress, organise files, document test results, and use tools such as GitHub and Jira-style task tracking. These skills were important because the ERS project included many connected parts. If the work was not organised clearly, it would be difficult to test, debug, and continue development. This helped me understand that engineering projects require both technical ability and good working habits.

Overall, this placement strengthened my connection between academic learning and future career development. It helped me understand how my degree can lead to work in IoT systems, embedded development, communication technology, system integration, and digital solutions. The experience also showed me the type of skills employers may expect from engineering graduates, such as problem-solving, documentation, teamwork, testing, and the ability to learn new tools quickly. This has given me a stronger foundation and more confidence for my future career in engineering and technology.

## Feedback on the Organisation / Overall satisfaction

Overall, I was very satisfied with my placement experience at Micromax. The company provided a supportive and positive working environment, which helped me feel comfortable asking questions, learning new skills, and taking part in a real engineering project. During the placement, I was not only completing simple tasks, but also working on practical problems that were connected to real workplace needs. This made the experience meaningful and helped me understand how engineering work is carried out in an industry environment.

One of the most positive parts of this placement was the support I received from my mentor and teammates. Before starting each major stage of the project, my mentor usually guided us to discuss the overall plan, expected outcomes, possible challenges, and task arrangement. This helped me work with a clearer direction instead of starting without a proper structure. When I met technical difficulties, my mentor also helped me analyse the problem step by step, test possible solutions, and understand the reason behind the issue. This process improved both my technical skills and my confidence in solving problems.

The company also provided strong practical support for the project. For example, when the project required specific hardware or testing equipment, the company was willing to purchase and provide the necessary devices. This was very important because the Emergency Response System involved real hardware testing, such as Raspberry Pi devices, sensors, communication modules, gateways, and alert components. With this support, I was able to test the system in a more realistic way and better understand the difference between theoretical design and practical implementation.

I also appreciated the working culture at Micromax. The team environment was friendly, open, and helpful. I felt that I could ask questions when I was unsure, and I could discuss ideas with my mentor and teammates. This type of environment made learning easier and reduced the pressure of facing new technical challenges. It also helped me understand that teamwork and communication are very important in engineering projects, especially when the project includes both hardware and software parts.

This placement met my expectations and gave me a valuable opportunity to grow. I was able to apply my university knowledge to a real project, develop practical skills, improve my working habits, and gain a clearer understanding of my future career direction. I also learned how important it is to plan before starting a task, document progress clearly, test carefully, and communicate problems early. These are useful habits that I believe will continue to help me in future engineering work.

Overall, I would highly recommend Micromax as a placement company for students who are interested in engineering, IoT, embedded systems, and practical technology projects. The company provides real project experience, good mentorship, a supportive team environment, and enough resources for students to learn through practice. For me, this placement was a very positive experience and an important step in preparing for my future career.

# **Conclusion**

Overall, my placement at Micromax was a valuable and meaningful experience. Through the Emergency Response System project, I was able to take part in a real engineering project that was connected to workplace safety and practical user needs. This experience helped me understand how an engineering idea can be developed into a working prototype through planning, testing, debugging, and continuous improvement.

During the placement, I improved both my technical and professional skills. Technically, I gained more experience in embedded systems, IoT communication, server-side programming, database logging, alert workflows, and indoor location estimation. Professionally, I developed better habits in task planning, daily summaries, documentation, teamwork, and communication. These skills are important because real engineering work requires not only technical knowledge, but also clear organisation and effective collaboration.

This placement also strengthened the connection between my academic studies and future career direction. It allowed me to apply knowledge from my degree to a practical project and showed me the importance of solving real problems, not only completing theoretical exercises. It also increased my interest in IoT systems, embedded development, communication technology, and system integration.

In conclusion, this placement has been an important step in my academic and professional development. It gave me practical industry experience, helped me build confidence, and prepared me better for future engineering roles. I believe the skills and insights I gained from Micromax will continue to support my future study and career development.
